MAINTAINING.md:21:- **technical-writing** — writes, revises and reviews technical documents (README, how-to guide, tutorial, reference, concept page, runbook, release notes, changelog entry, pull request description; a commit message only when the user asks for help with one, since the description leaves it out so that a request to commit does not fire the skill). The body is a procedure (reader, job, facts, draft, actor pass, `unslop`, check) followed by rules in five layers (document, paragraph, sentence, words, procedures and samples); the per-document guidance and the before/after pairs sit in `references/documents.md` and `references/actors.md`. The rule the skill exists for is the first of its contract: **every verb has an actor**, written as the subject of an active verb. It follows a passage of Tanya Reilly's *The Staff Engineer's Path* that the repository's author read in the book and supplied; the same passage quotes Rebecca Johnson's test. The book was not consulted while the skill was written, and no sentence or example of it is in the skill. The rule is about information and not about grammar, and that is what keeps it from contradicting `explain`, whose research found that a nested clause costs the reader more than a passive: a passive that names its actor loses only directness, a passive without one drops a fact. The detector for the grammatical passive is Rebecca Johnson's "by zombies" test, in step 4 and in `references/actors.md`; the skill says next to it that the test finds one of the six hiding places and also fits a state, so that it does not replace the question asked of every verb. Two passives stay (the actor is unknown and the text says so; the verb describes a state). A third, the passive that names its actor with "by" in a paragraph about the object, was in the draft because Gopen and Swan make the case for it, and the author removed it before release: it was the one exception with no checkable criterion, it contradicted the rule as stated, and an active verb keeps the object at the front just as well ("the request then goes to the gateway, which signs it"; `references/actors.md` has the pairs). Do not put it back as a readability fix. Its form of the shared contract is "look the actor up, never pick one": it is a document-writing skill, so it asks, but only after reading the repository, and the same rule covers every command, flag, path, default and output (copied from the repository or from a run that changes nothing; what was not run is listed in the reply). In a revision a passive whose actor the repository does not give **stays as written** and becomes a question, where `unslop` would delete the claim: the two skills differ here on purpose, because this one can read the source and that one edits a text alone. It owns no typography rule and no list of machine-writing patterns; it invokes `unslop`, when installed, after the actor pass. Other skills may call it as they call `unslop`, and then it applies only the actor pass and the rules for the sentence and the words, before `unslop`, and reports nothing. None calls it today: `design-doc` did in 1.7.0 and stopped in 1.8.0 (see its note). `adr` does not call it: a record is short, its Decision is already "We will …", and `unslop` S17 covers the rest for less context. `explain` does not call it either: its texts are messages, and its explanations are kept away even from `unslop`. The description is automatic and borders `explain` ("make this clearer") and `design-doc`; the sweep below checks that it does not fire on their requests, and not which skill wins when both are installed, because the harness loads only the candidate. One case of both installed was probed, `technical-writing-workspace/trigger-evals/border-design-doc-2026-11-22/` (2026-11-22, claude-sonnet-5-5): eval 9 of `design-doc` ("Atualiza a documentação" for a design doc of a system in production), eight sessions with `design-doc` and `unslop` loaded as plugins and eight with `technical-writing` added. No session invoked any skill, in either cell, so this skill does not take that request and its description needs no exclusion for it; what the probe found is a miss of `design-doc`'s description (see its note). A first attempt of the same probe, and the eight eval 9 sessions of `design-doc-workspace/iteration-27/`, had the skills inside the project, where a session finds their files with `git ls-files` and reads them without the Skill tool: the four of eight in which this skill fired there are not a trigger count. To count invocations with several skills installed, load each plugin with `--plugin-dir` from outside the project and run a canary. Whether the skill is reached at all when the file is in the project, which the trigger harness cannot show, was probed the same way (`technical-writing-workspace/trigger-evals/in-project-2026-11-22/`, claude-sonnet-5-5, four sessions per request, `technical-writing` and `unslop` installed): it was invoked in 20 of 20 sessions on the five evals that have a fixture and in 4 of 4 on the pasted diff, as the first tool call except on the review, where the session reads the file first. It is not consulted for a change of one value in an existing page ("subimos o limite pra 250 mil linhas, atualiza a documentação": 0 of 8, 1 of 24 with the sessions of the `design-doc` probe), where the session edits the number and says so. The description was left as it is: unlike the one-line change that `code-comments` claims, nothing in this skill's checks says what it would add there. Decisions that are easy to undo by accident: a new document follows the language of the repository's docs directory when one exists with documents in it, and the language of the conversation otherwise (the author's decision of 2026-11-22; a lone README in another language does not set the language, and a request that names a language wins either way); no limit counted in words (the pstack original has them; Gopen and Swan argue length is not the defect, and `explain` already refuses numbers it cannot support); no pair or example copied from a source (all were written for the skill, and `NOTICE.md` says so); Portuguese is covered in `references/actors.md` because the forms with "se" hide the actor in a way an English-only rule misses. No external tooling. The eval set and the trigger eval set are written (`technical-writing-workspace/evals/evals.json`, `technical-writing-workspace/trigger-evals/trigger_eval.json`); the eval set has 121 frozen checks (`technical-writing-workspace/evals/checks-baseline.json`) and a first A/B, `technical-writing-workspace/iteration-1/` (2026-11-22, claude-sonnet-5-5, two runs per cell): 231/242 checks met with the skill read against 203/242 without it. The actor pass on a revision is not what separates the cells: in eval 1 every run of both named each actor from the code, left the backups without one and asked who rotates them. What separates, in both runs each way, is reading the repository before writing a new document (without the skill both runs of eval 3 wrote a generic runbook without opening a file, so the threshold and the requeue script are placeholders and a 30-minute escalation limit appears that nobody gave), the shape of a review (questions apart from edits, the mix of document kinds named) and of a pull request description (what the change does before why, how to verify it), and a new README with no agentless passive about the pipeline. Two things count against the skill. Both of its READMEs carry a "License and help" heading over a TODO, which eval 2 asks not to appear: it comes from item 5 of the README entry in `references/documents.md`. And the rule of at most three lines on what changed, with no summary of the document, failed in both skill runs of eval 1, as it did without the skill and as it did for `explain`. Both cells left the good guide of eval 6 untouched. Two runs measure no rate, the brief told the executor to read the skill, and `unslop` was not installed, so step 5 never ran. 1.0.1 answers those two things, and `technical-writing-workspace/iteration-2/` ran evals 1 and 2 four times on it, with the 1.0.0 runs re-judged in the same batch. The README entry now says that the parts for contributors and for license and help go in only when the repository states them: no README of 1.0.1 has the section (4/4 against 0/2). The three-line rule is repeated in the check list of step 5, and its two checks did not move (1/4 and 0/4): the replies got shorter, four or five lines against seven and nine, but each still names what every component does in one sentence, which the judges read as the document retold. Do not count that rule as followed. The same batch shows a small miss of the skill's own rule: "Once the upload is done", the fixture's clause, survives in five of six skill documents, and the judges split on whether it is a passive or a state. Check 1.26 was reworded by a dated amendment after iteration-1, because as frozen it failed a document for figures that are in the fixture. The trigger set has one routine check, of 2026-11-22 on claude-sonnet-5-5 (Claude Code 2.1.330, one sweep, 3 runs per query, `technical-writing-workspace/trigger-evals/serial-2026-11-22-routine-sonnet.json`): 0/30 false fires with the canary at 3/3, including a design doc, a decision to record, an explanation, an email, `unslop` by name, a diagram, docstrings, a translation, a blog post and "commit what's staged and push"; and 24/30 on the positives. The six misses are two queries at 0/3, and both came from the query: one said "this repo has no README" and pointed at a Makefile, the other asked for an entry in a CHANGELOG, and this repository has a README, no Makefile and no CHANGELOG. Three captured sessions each (`transcripts-readme-miss-sonnet/`, `transcripts-changelog-miss-sonnet/` there) searched the repository and replied that the premises do not hold, with nothing left to write. The set now carries the project and the changelog in the message; probed the same day at five runs each, those two queries fired 5/5 and 4/5 as the first tool call (`transcripts-readme-reworded-sonnet-n5/`, `transcripts-changelog-reworded-sonnet-n5/`; the miss answered the one-line entry in prose). The first full sweeps on the set as it now stands are of 2026-11-22 (`README-full-sweep-2026-11-22.md` there): 30/30 on the positives, 0/30 false fires and the canary at 3/3 on claude-sonnet-5-5, and on claude-haiku-5-5 11/50 on the positives (seven of ten never fire) with 0/30 false fires and the canary at 3/3. That is the lowest haiku number of the five skills that have one, and no transcript says why; it is an early warning and the description was not tuned to it. Before that A/B there were three smoke sessions of 2026-11-22 (subagents on the `sonnet` alias, fixture copies outside the repository, outputs not kept), which measure nothing: on eval 1 both the session that read the skill and the one that did not named every actor from the code and left the backup sentence without one, and the difference was scope (the skill kept the four sections; the baseline renamed them and added a diagram, a table and a section); on eval 3 the session wrote the runbook in English because the fixture's one doc is in English, left `TODO` marks for the escalation contacts instead of inventing them, and stated as fact a few things the fixture does not show (a management UI, "the dead messages share one cause in most incidents"). Two sentences of 1.0.0 answer that run: contract 2 now covers behavior, and step 3 says what a hole looks like when the user wants the document before answering.

The upload handler isn't in this repository. `skills` contains only Markdown skills and eval tooling, and a search for `upload`, `413`, `OPS-412` and `test_upload_rejects` found nothing relevant. So the description below is written from your summary, not from the diff. Check the file names and the test before you post it.

**Title:** Reject upload bodies over 1 MB with 413 and stop reading them whole into memory

**Description:**

Fixes OPS-412. Production instances were being OOM-killed because the upload handler read the whole request body into memory before checking its size.

**What changes**

- The upload handler rejects a request body larger than 1 MB with `413 Payload Too Large`.
- The handler streams the body instead of reading it all into memory, so memory use no longer grows with the size of the upload.

**Testing**

- Added `test_upload_rejects_body_above_limit`, which sends a body over the limit and checks for a 413.
- Run the test suite locally before merging.

Refs: OPS-412
